questions.stem: Which statement about the rule of twelfths is correct?
options: It is exact for every tide, so it can replace the tables
It only works for diurnal tides
It applies to the stream speed rather than the height
It is a rough approximation that assumes a smooth rise or fall of about six hours, so use the published method when accuracy matters
questions.explanation: The rule splits a rise or fall into six periods covering 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12 and 1/12 of the range. It assumes a smooth curve and a regular duration, so it is a rough estimate only. It is not exact and it is about the height, not the stream. Use the CHS method and a safety margin for real decisions.

questions.stem: Invented figures: low water at 0600 is 0.6 m and the next high water at 1200 is 4.2 m. Using the rule of twelfths, what is the height of tide at 1000?
questions.explanation: Range = 4.2 - 0.6 = 3.6 m, so one twelfth is 0.3 m. Four hours after low water the running total is 9/12, which is 9 x 0.3 = 2.7 m of rise. Height = 0.6 + 2.7 = 3.3 m. A straight-line estimate would give 3.0 m, which is too low, 3.9 m is the 1100 value, and 1.8 m comes from using 4/12 instead of 9/12.

questions.stem: Same invented tide: low water at 0600 is 0.6 m and high water at 1200 is 4.2 m. Using the rule of twelfths, with the running total of 3/12 at 0800 and 6/12 at 0900 and splitting the hour evenly, about what is the height at 0830?
questions.explanation: Halfway between 3/12 at 0800 and 6/12 at 0900 is 4.5/12. 4.5 x 0.3 m = 1.35 m of rise, so the height is 0.6 + 1.35 = 1.95 m. A straight line from low to high water would give 2.1 m, which is not what the rule says. 2.4 m is the 0900 value and 1.8 m is below the 0830 value.

questions.stem: Invented figures: a shoal has a charted sounding of 1.5 m. At 0900 the height of tide is 2.4 m. Your draft is 1.8 m. How much water is there under your keel over the shoal at 0900?
questions.explanation: Depth = charted depth + height of tide = 1.5 + 2.4 = 3.9 m. Under the keel = depth - draft = 3.9 - 1.8 = 2.1 m. 0.6 m (2.4 - 1.8) forgets the charted depth. 3.9 m is the depth, not the clearance under the keel. 5.7 m adds the draft instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: Invented figures: a shoal has a charted sounding of 1.0 m. Your draft is 1.8 m and you want 1.2 m under the keel. The tide rises from low water 0.6 m at 0600 to high water 4.2 m at 1200. Using the rule of twelfths at whole hours (0.9 m at 0700, 1.5 m at 0800, 2.4 m at 0900, 3.3 m at 1000, 3.9 m at 1100), what is the first whole hour with enough water?
questions.explanation: Depth needed = 1.8 + 1.2 = 3.0 m. Height of tide needed = 3.0 - 1.0 = 2.0 m. At 0800 the height is only 1.5 m, which is not enough. At 0900 it is 2.4 m, which is enough. So 0900 is the first whole hour. In practice, allow a safety margin because the rule is only an estimate.

questions.stem: Invented figures: a reference port has low water at 0715 with a height of 0.8 m. The correction for a secondary port is a time difference of plus 0 h 50 min and a height difference of minus 0.2 m. What are the secondary port's low water time and height?
questions.explanation: Apply each difference with its sign: 0715 + 0 h 50 min = 0805, and 0.8 m - 0.2 m = 0.6 m. The other options reverse the sign of the time difference, the height difference, or both. Always check the instructions in the actual publication, because the format of the corrections can differ.

questions.stem: Invented scenario: a tide table states that its times are in standard time. Daylight saving time is in effect, and the table shows high water at 1400. At what time on the clocks aboard will high water occur?
questions.explanation: Daylight saving time is one hour ahead of standard time, so you add one hour: 1400 becomes 1500 on the clocks aboard. Subtracting gives 1300, and ignoring the difference (1400) is the classic error. Adding two hours (1600) is also wrong. Always check which time standard your actual edition uses.

questions.stem: What does a tide table give for each day at a reference port, and what are its heights measured from?
options: The times and heights of high and low waters, with heights measured up from chart datum
The speed and direction of the tidal stream, measured in knots
Only the time of high water, with heights measured from mean sea level
The depth of water over every shoal in the area
questions.explanation: A tide table lists the times and heights of the high and low waters, and the heights are measured up from chart datum. Stream speeds and directions are in the current tables. A tide table does not give depths over shoals: you add the height of tide to the charted depth yourself.

questions.stem: Using the rule of twelfths on a regular rise lasting about six hours, how much of the range has the water covered three hours after low water?
questions.explanation: The shares for the six periods are 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths. After three periods the running total is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 twelfths, half the range. A quarter (3/12) is the total after two periods, and three quarters (9/12) after four.

questions.stem: A strong onshore gale and very low air pressure have lasted for two days. How should you treat the predicted heights in the tide table?
options: As exact, because tide tables already include the weather
As a baseline only, because wind and air pressure can make the actual height differ from the prediction
As useless, because tide tables only work in calm weather
As accurate only for diurnal tides
questions.explanation: Tide tables are astronomical predictions and do not include the weather. Strong winds, big changes in air pressure and heavy river flow can make the real height differ, sometimes by a lot. The table is still the starting point; you allow for the weather and look at what the water is actually doing.
